name: Pink
lede: Pink is pale red, the only basic English color word that names part of another one. The ancients saw it but never named it, Europe filed it as a kind of yellow for three centuries, it fades faster than almost any other paint, and it became a girls' color only in the twentieth century.

sections.title: A word for a pale red
sections.body:
Pink is the light end of [[red]], and English is unusual in giving it a word of its own [11]. Batchelor points out that it is the only basic English color term that names part of another basic term; light blue is as distinct from dark blue, yet English has no separate word for it, while Russian does [11]. In Berlin and Kay's 1969 survey, pink was among the last basic terms a language acquires [11]. Critics say that ordering is overstated [12].

The ancients saw pink in flowers, stones and dawn skies, but Greek and Latin had no adjective for it [1]. The Latin *roseus* is a false friend: it meant bright red or vermilion, and Pastoureau reads Homer's rosy-fingered dawn as a red glow [1]. In medieval Latin *roseus* still meant vermilion and was used for cheeks, lips and make-up, while Old French *rose* meant pale or beige more often than pink [1].

Most Romance languages now use a word from the rose [5]. English took another route. The Oxford English Dictionary first records pink for pale reds in the late seventeenth century, and St Clair thinks the word probably came from the flower called the pink, *Dianthus plumarius*, though this is not certain [5].

sections.title: When pink was yellow
sections.body:
Before it named a color, pink named a paint. In the seventeenth century a pink was a pigment made by fixing a plant dye, from weld, broom or unripe buckthorn berries, onto chalk, alum or ground eggshell [22]. Pinks came in green, brown and rose, but most were yellow [22][5]. As late as 1830, Tingry's guide for house painters gave a recipe for a yellow paint called pink, made with woad [33].

Books disagree on what the English noun first meant [22][1]. Ball and St Clair describe it as this type of pigment, of any color [22][5]; Pastoureau says English pink long meant only the dyestuff of brazilwood, before it came to name the color the wood gave [1]. Ball's account bridges the two: rose pink, the pink made from brazilwood, was one kind among many, and as yellow pink fell out of use in the late eighteenth century the word slid onto [[rose-pink]] alone [22].

sections.title: Carnation: a new color for princes
sections.body:
Pink as a fashion began with a dye. Around 1380 to 1400, Italian dyers found new mordants that made brazilwood, an Asian dyewood long thought unreliable, give stable pinks, and the new shades became a craze [1][2]. Pastoureau names Jean de Berry among the first princes to dress in them [26].

The color needed a name. Venetian and Tuscan dyers borrowed *incarnato*, until then a word for a person's complexion: French had *incarnat* by about 1400 to 1420, Castilian had *encarnado*, and English had [[carnation]] [1]. But where did it belong? Aristotle's order of colors, still standard, ran from white through yellow to red, so the place between white and red was taken [1]. From the fifteenth to the seventeenth century, dictionaries and color manuals therefore treated carnation as a pale, delicate shade of [[yellow]] [1].

Renaissance writers loved it anyway. In 1528 the humanist Antonio Telesio called pink the most beautiful color, and in 1557 Lodovico Dolce named white, pink and green a perfect harmony [3]. Three centuries earlier Vincent of Beauvais had already argued that a pink, much white with a little red, pleases the eye the way a musical fifth pleases the ear [4].

The modern pink arrived in the mid-eighteenth century. Madame de Pompadour made pink and sky blue the rage of the French court, men wore pink as freely as women, and pink was at last seen as red mixed with white [1]. St Clair adds that Pompadour helped make bright pink Sèvres porcelain fashionable [5]. Even so, the French adjective *rose* entered the Académie's dictionary only in 1835 [1].

sections.title: Pink in cloth
sections.body:
Pink is older in cloth than in words. Among the oldest known flax fibres, from a cave in Georgia in the Caucasus, is a piece about 23,000 years old that was once pink [7]. A child's burial at Qingtai in China, about five thousand years old, held a pink silk gauze; experts there think it was dyed with iron ore [8]. A madder-dyed cotton scrap from Mohenjo-daro, about 4,600 years old, would have been pink or orange-red depending on its mordant [9].

Dyers had several routes to pink. The Incas used brazilwood for deep pinks [15]. Safflower, which gives yellow in an alkaline bath and a crimson pink in an acid one, dyed the original red tape tied around English legal papers [16]. Cochineal gave soft, fast pinks [17], and it lasted into the kitchen: in Nesbit's *The Railway Children* (1906), pink icing is colored with a few drops of it [18]. Roman painters, working in paint rather than dye, made pinks by burning white lead together with red ochre [24].

sections.title: The color that fades
sections.body:
Pink is the color most likely to be missing from an old painting. Painters' pinks were usually lakes, dyes fixed on a colorless base, and lakes fade in light [14][27]. Van Gogh's *[[art:nga-72328|Roses]]* at the National Gallery of Art in Washington was long called *White Roses*, until traces of what was probably madder red showed that the roses had been pink [13]. Van Gogh also favored a pink lake made from eosin, a coal-tar dye that BASF sold from 1874, and it has damaged some of his works [14]. Greenfield describes geranium pink lakes of the period fading to pale blue and lavender-white [18].

The pattern repeats across centuries. The deathly pale face in Reynolds's portrait of Anne, Countess of Albemarle, was once pinker, before its red lake, probably cochineal, drained away [27]. Mark Rothko's murals for Harvard, given in 1962, were ruined by 1979: their dark pinks and crimsons included a fugitive red, and parts turned light blue [28]. In the Dunhuang caves, figures painted pale pink with lead white and red lead have turned black [29].

Fading can also reveal what lies underneath. Medieval painters laid flesh over an underlayer of green earth, and where the pink above has faded, the saints' faces now look green [19]. Cennino Cennini advised leaving the pink off entirely when painting a corpse [19]. Look for that green in the faces of early panel paintings: it is a pink that has gone.

sections.title: Pink for girls, a recent rule
sections.body:
The idea that pink has always been for girls is a myth. In 1893 a New York Times article on baby clothes gave the rule as pink for boys and blue for girls, and in 1918 a trade publication still called pink the stronger color, better suited to boys [5]. Pink was faded red, and red was then the color of soldiers and cardinals [5]. Until about 1900, children under two of both sexes usually wore white [5].

Pastoureau traces the change. Pink and sky blue for babies appeared in the English-speaking world in the mid-nineteenth century, without a gender rule, and before the First World War boys were, if anything, dressed in pink more often [1]. Only in the 1930s, when fabrics that survived boiling washes made pastel baby clothes practical, did pink for girls and blue for boys take hold, first in the United States [1]. Pastoureau also rejects the claim that the custom came from the Virgin's protection [1]. From the 1970s the Barbie doll fixed the association [1].

sections.title: Shocking, calming, hiding
sections.body:
In 1937 the designer Elsa Schiaparelli launched her perfume *Shocking* and the vivid pink that went with it, taking the color from the 17.47-carat pink diamond Tête de Bélier worn by the heiress Daisy Fellowes [6]. That [[shocking-pink|shocking pink]] became the pink of strong-willed twentieth-century women, from Schiaparelli to Marilyn Monroe [5].

A later pink made bolder claims. In 1979 Alexander Schauss reported that a particular bright pink sapped men's strength, after two officers at a naval prison in Seattle, Gene Baker and Ron Miller, painted a holding cell with it [20]. The claim that Baker-Miller pink calms aggression did not survive testing: later studies were contradictory, a 1988 study found no effect on strength or blood pressure [20], and Eckstut calls the prison studies debunked [21]. Our library files the shade as [[schauss-pink]], about three units from this page's swatch [35].

Pink has also been used to hide. In 1940 Lord Mountbatten had his destroyers painted a greyish [[mountbatten-pink]] after watching a liner with a pinkish hull vanish at dusk; it was phased out by 1942, and whether it worked is unproven [10]. The Nazis marked gay men in the camps with a pink triangle, a symbol later reclaimed [23]. Pink is almost absent from national flags [25]. And, as Pastoureau notes, Europe's pigs were mostly black until crossbreeding with Asian breeds turned them [[pig-pink|pink]] [31].

sections.title: How pink works
sections.body:
Pink is not in the rainbow. A pink surface reflects all wavelengths of light, red more strongly than the rest: it is white light with extra red, not a weak spectral color [30]. Pink and [[maroon]] differ only in lightness, just as yellow and brown do [32].

Painters meet pink's oddities in the mixing. Adding white to a red tends to push it toward [[magenta]], while a thin transparent layer of red over a white ground gives a cleaner pink [34]. The painter Gurney found red neon impossible to mix: a tint light enough to match its brightness was weak in chroma and looked orange or pink [41]. John Dalton, describing his own color blindness in 1794, wrote that a pink geranium looked blue to him by day and red by candlelight; Livingstone calls it the first systematic account of color blindness [32]. And hot pink beside tangerine, two colors of equal lightness, makes a surface seem to jitter [37].

sections.title: Roses, rubies and pearls
sections.body:
Even the rose had to become pink. Ancient and medieval roses were red or white, and truly rose-colored roses spread only as gardeners bred new varieties [24][1]. In Burma the grades of ruby run from pigeon's blood down to pink like a flower, and buyers at Mogok sit under pink umbrellas, because light through pink canvas makes rubies look brighter [38]. Morganite, a pink beryl found in Madagascar in 1911 and named after the banker J. P. Morgan, owes its color to manganese [39].

The teaching point is simple: in nature, most pinks are thin. Petals, skin, a pearl's sheen and a dawn sky all let white show through red, which is also why pink is so hard to keep in paint.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This is the emptiest result in our archive. Across 23,781 paintings, each summarized by its six largest area colors, not one area color comes within eight units of this pink [35]. The nearest is 8.9 units away, in Odilon Redon's *[[art:commons-Q17491525|Fleurs]]* [35]. Widen the net to ten units and four paintings qualify, led by a Rajput portrait, *[[art:cma-314454|Maharana Jawan Singh of Mewar Holding a Falcon]]*, of about 1835, where an area our palette names [[puce]] covers 40 per cent of the page [35]. Matisse's *[[art:smk-KMSr171|Portrait of Madame Matisse (The Green Line)]]* of 1905 is another [35].

Pink is everywhere in painting, in cheeks, petals and skies, so why the gap? The pinks are small, and six area colors average them into their surroundings [35]. They are also the colors most likely to have faded, as the paintings above show [14][27]. Of the 145 light, pink-hued area colors in the whole archive, only one reaches a chroma of 30; this swatch's chroma is 43 [35]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [35].

The swatch here is a moderate purplish pink. The CSS keyword `pink` is much paler, about 13 units away, and [[hot-pink]] about 8 [36]. Our nearest named neighbors are Schauss Pink (3.4 units), [[amaranth-pink]] (3.5) and Pig Pink (3.7) [36]. In Google Books the word *pink* has risen almost steadily, from about 16 per cent of its peak in 1800 to the peak itself in 2016 [40].

questions.q: Why do the faces in some early Italian panel paintings look greenish today?
choices: The pink flesh paint has faded, letting the green-earth underlayer show through
Painters showed saints as sickly on purpose
Green varnish was applied in the nineteenth century
Museum lighting turns pink to green
questions.answer: The pink flesh paint has faded, letting the green-earth underlayer show through

openers: In the 1600s most paints called pink were yellow.
